context.transcript_excerpt: Welcome to the Prosperity Podcast with me, Nicole Bremner, an investor and entrepreneur. Along with discussions around investing, I'm currently serializing my book, Bricked It, the story of building and losing a multi-million pound property portfolio. Let's get into it. Chapter 7, The Safer System. Learn from the mistakes of others. You can't live long enough to make them all yourself. Eleanor Roosevelt. I developed the safer system because with over a decade of experience and owning over 110 properties at one stage, I've made just about every mistake possible. This is not about investing into an asset and hoping it will turn to gold. It's applying a long term strategy to every investment decision to ensure that it meets your objectives now and in the future. Most importantly, it's about making sure that your investments work for you and not you for them. You should work through these steps in their entirety before you enter into an investment. Sure, you could decide on your strategy, then go out and acquire while thinking about your funding and exit. But that's not safe. The safer system considers each of these steps before you enter into that investment. I know what trouble you can get into if you rely solely on hope, not facts. I'll outline each element of the safer system before illustrating it in practice with a real life example. Safer. Strategy. What is your overall investment strategy? What do you need your portfolio to do for you? The focus here is not what you need to build your portfolio, but what your portfolio needs to earn to give you the lifestyle that you desire. Once you have your strategy, let's look at the four major pillars of investments individually. Cash, equities, property and pension assets. How do these fit into your strategy based on expenses, time horizon and appetite for risk? Are you holding too much cash? Usually it's not enough, but could you cover three months of expenses if something happened? If you don't have medical insurance, do you have the cash available to cover an emergency? What about property? Is your portfolio serving you or have you bought yourself a low paying job? More on that later, but for now, remember that your home is part of your investment portfolio. Most of us have too much money tied up in property, given that it's often our largest financial asset. Let's say that you are property obsessed, I get it, and you want to invest in additional property. What is the best strategy for you? Buy to let? Developing? Short or holiday lets? Perhaps purchase lease options or planning gain? What about location? That could be a whole separate section. There are so many options to choose from. Your circumstances, including your available cash, time constraints and tax situation will determine which strategy is right for you. What about angel investing, crypto or even luxury handbags? These speculative investments can have a place in a portfolio. It's exciting to speculate on currencies. My teenage boys spend all their free time and free cash doing it. But once you're an adult with adult responsibilities, speculative investments should be limited, very limited, and only considered if the other pillars of your investment portfolio are solid. A rule of thumb is that speculative investments should not make up more than about 5% of your net assets. Speculative investments are high-risk assets purchased with the hope of achieving substantial short-term profits, but with a significant chance of loss. They typically lack reliable fundamentals, generate little or no income, and depend heavily on price movements driven by market sentiment, hype, or unpredictable factors. pending_qa.q: What happened in a cautionary case where a property developer faced 2% monthly interest rates from private investors?
pending_qa.r: In 2017, Pete overstretched on a development and borrowed too much from loan shark-like private investors at 2% per month interest payments. His project overran and he could no longer keep up payments. One investor was threatening to seize control if his loan was not repaid in seven days. Pete's 83-year-old mother had given him 113,000 pounds—everything his parents had squirreled away for life—and it was lost when the investor exercised his rights to take the project. The investor could have shown clemency and allowed Pete to work his way out, but instead chose to exercise his rights completely.

pending_qa.q: What tax and penalty risks arise from misunderstanding fixed-term savings account terms?
pending_qa.r: Stuart obtained a six-month 0% cash transfer of £5,000 from his credit card company and noticed his bank was offering 12-month fixed rate of 5.1% on savings accounts. He did not read the fine print—the deposits were fixed, meaning he could not withdraw without penalties. He invested the £5,000 at 5.1% for 12 months thinking he had an arbitrage opportunity. Six months passed with interest accruing, but then the credit card company started direct debits for interest on the £5,000 at 23.9%, which he could not afford. He had to withdraw early, forfeit all earned interest and pay off the credit card immediately.

pending_qa.q: How does inheritance tax apply to residential property held in limited companies?
pending_qa.r: Property held in a limited company is not protected from Inheritance Tax (IHT). The deceased's share of the business assets form part of their estate and are liable for inheritance tax if applicable. Nicole initially argued incorrectly with financial advisor Paul that her property was fine because it was in limited companies, but this is a common misconception among property investors. Owning property in limited companies does not mitigate IHT.

pending_qa.q: What inheritance tax burden did two beneficiaries face from a £5,500,000 property portfolio?
pending_qa.r: Two clients inherited an unencumbered portfolio of properties in central London worth approximately £5,500,000 from their deceased mother. HMRC was demanding Inheritance Tax of £2,200,000. While they were desperate to retain the assets and continue running the commercial properties, they ultimately decided it was too risky to take on that level of debt to raise finance against the properties, so they chose to sell down part of the portfolio and pay the taxes.

pending_qa.q: What monthly investment compound interest benchmark leads to millionaire status in 30 years?
pending_qa.r: Some of the most successful investors put aside a set amount of money every single month. Put aside £1,000 a month and in 30 years you will have £1,500,000 assuming an 8% per annum return. Increase it to £1,200 a month and you will get to £1,800,000. With £1,500 a month spare, it could be worth £2,250,000. However, timing matters significantly—£2,250,000 is great if you start when you are 20 and by 50 can spend the rest of your life enjoying it, but not as great if you start when you are 50 and save by 80.

pending_qa.q: What structural and financial challenges did a property investor named Barbara face with her portfolio?
pending_qa.r: Barbara, age 53, single with no children, no home, no savings and no pension, owned six properties worth £700,000 before debt and £500,000 after debt in Sheffield and Doncaster. She received £4,000 per month gross rental income but only £2,000 after mortgage repayments and tax. She had not factored in £6,000 per year in maintenance costs or her time spent on properties. Her properties would incur approximately £140,000 in Capital Gains Tax if sold, meaning her £700,000 portfolio was actually worth £560,000 after tax. Her property loans at 2.5% needed refinancing to 4-5% in 10 months. She was living in shared accommodation paying £450 per month but would face £1,200 per month rent plus £800 bills once her ex sold their shared flat.

pending_qa.q: What radical restructuring solution was recommended for Barbara's unsustainable property portfolio situation?
pending_qa.r: Nicole suggested Barbara sell everything—every last property—pay the Capital Gains Tax, and pay off her car loan too. By doing this, she would net £350,000 in cash. £300,000 could be used to buy a lovely two-bed property in the area she desires, providing her with a home and financial stability, rather than continuing to be enslaved by a portfolio that was actually worth only £560,000 after tax and debt while generating insufficient net income to cover her rising living costs and upcoming refinancing requirements.
